answer: From 1985 onwards, respondents in the Non-Black Non-Hispanic cohort (cohort==3, used as ~White proxy) had substantially higher median Family net wealth than Black (cohort==1) and Hispanic (cohort==2) respondents, in every wave (1985, 1990, 1996) and in both per-year available-case and balanced sub-sample analyses. Headline medians: 1985 ~White-proxy $3,500 (n=5,774) vs Black $1,600 (n=1,699) vs Hispanic $500 (n=2,631); 1990 $12,972 (n=5,336) vs $4,800 (n=1,528) vs $1,600 (n=2,431); 1996 $42,600 (n=3,557) vs $9,800 (n=1,368) vs $2,562.5 (n=2,114). The cohort rank-ordering is preserved in the balanced sub-sample (n=5,739; Black 1,084, Hispanic 1,723, ~White-proxy 2,932), with 1996 balanced medians $42,600 / $9,075 / $2,400. In 1996, the median Black household's wealth was ~23% and the median Hispanic household's was ~6% of the median ~White-proxy household's wealth. Explicit caveats: cohort-code mapping is 1:BLACK, 2:HISPANIC, 3:NON-BLACK NON-HISPANIC (verbatim from the raw CSV header); no sampling-weight variable exists in data/nls_raw.csv (only body-weight kg columns), so all medians are unweighted; figures are family-level nominal dollars; only the three supplied waves (1985, 1990, 1996) are reported; no CPI deflation, no winsorization, top-coding, or log-transform applied to the headline.

payload.hypothesis: From 1985 onwards, the median Family net wealth of the Non-Black Non-Hispanic cohort (cohort==3, used here as a ~White proxy because the codebook does not isolate non-Hispanic Whites) is substantially higher than that of the Black (cohort==1) and Hispanic (cohort==2) cohorts in NLSY79, in every wealth snapshot available in the file (1985, 1990, 1996) and in both per-year available-case and balanced sub-sample analyses. In nominal dollars, 1996 medians are $42,600 (White-proxy, n=3,557) vs $9,800 (Black, n=1,368) vs $2,562.5 (Hispanic, n=2,114); in 1996 the median Black household holds ~23% and the median Hispanic household ~6% of the median White-proxy household's wealth. The cohort rank-ordering ~White-proxy > Black > Hispanic and the widening absolute and relative gap are robust to attrition handling. Caveats: cohort==3 is only an approximation to White (it also includes Asians, Native Americans, and mixed/other respondents); there is no sampling-weight variable in data/nls_raw.csv so all medians are unweighted; figures are family-level nominal dollars; only the three supplied waves (1985, 1990, 1996) are reported; no CPI deflation, no winsorization, top-coding, or log-transform applied to the headline.
